## Claims — grouped by pericope

### 3:1–7 (Paul's role in administering the mystery)

- **[3:1]** Paul opens with emphatic self-reference to imprisonment, ἐγὼ Παῦλος ὁ δέσμιος (egō Paulos ho desmios, "I, Paul, the prisoner"). *Thielman:* the article on ὁ δέσμιος "places special emphasis on his imprisonment," adding "pathos and conviction to his prayer." Paul is prisoner "not of Rome but τοῦ Χριστου… and ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν (hyper hymōn tōn ethnōn, for you Gentiles)."
- **[3:1]** τούτου χάριν (toutou charin, "for this reason") — *Thielman:* points backward to 2:19–22 (Gentiles incorporated into God's dwelling), not forward to the prayer's substance; "'For this reason,' Paul the prisoner prays that his Gentile readers will grasp the vastness of Christ's love (3:16–19)."
- **[3:1–13]** *Thielman* frames 3:2–13 as a **digression**: "a reference to his suffering in the cause of the gospel in 3:1 prompts a reflection on his apostolic responsibility," and Paul signals return at 3:14 by repeating τούτου χάριν — analogous to 2 Cor. 2:14–7:4.
- **[3:1–7]** *Thielman* on authorship: "signs of extemporaneity, pathos… look genuine" — the false start in 3:1, lack of object for the three συν- prefixes in 3:6, the 105-word sentence "all look like a communication that was actually dictated with some emotion." He judges it "more likely that Paul himself was moved to speak this way as his secretary furiously took down his words."
- **[3:2]** οἰκονομία (oikonomia) "the responsibility of administering the grace of God given to me for you." *Thielman's* decision: here (unlike 3:9 = "administrative plan") οἰκονομία = "the responsibility that God has given to him to accomplish this task." Primary contemporary meaning was "management of a household" (LSJ), linking to the -οἰκ- terms of 2:19–22: "God has given him the responsibility of administering the part of his plan for the universe that involves the inclusion of the Gentiles within his household."
- **[3:2]** εἴ γε (ei ge, "if, as I assume") — *Thielman:* ambiguous particle implying both certainty and "some personal distance between Paul and his readers"; he takes it as evidence that "the real Paul dictated this letter" to "a wide audience of believers in Ephesus," many with "only a loose connection to him" after 7+ years' absence, ~5 in imprisonment.
- **[3:2, 7, 8]** *Subtheme (Thielman):* grace — Paul's task bracketed as "the grace of God given to me" (v.2) and "the gift of God's grace" (v.7a); he became "servant" only "by means of the effective working of God's power (v.7b)."
- **[3:3]** μυστήριον made known κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν (kata apocalypsin, "by revelation"). *Thielman:* κατά denotes **means**, not norm — "it came to him 'by revelation' from God." Analogy to **Dan. 2:17–19** (Daniel receiving Nebuchadnezzar's dream apart from his own cleverness, "strictly because God in his mercy revealed it"). "No amount of exegetical study of the Scriptures would have yielded this insight."
- **[3:3]** προέγραψα ἐν ὀλίγῳ ("I wrote briefly above") — *Thielman:* "Paul is probably describing what he has just written about the unity of Jews and Gentiles in Christ in 2:11–22," specifically the συν- compounds of 2:19–22. (Rejects Goodspeed's ten-letter-collection theory, Muddiman's Colossians, Sellin's Gal. 1:15–16.)
- **[3:4]** σύνεσις (synesis, "insight") — *Thielman:* not self-developed but God-given; δοθείσης and ἐγνωρίσθη are "divine passives," so "'my insight' here in 3:4" is rescued "from any element of boasting or egotism."
- **[3:4]** First-person claims of insight — *Thielman* (following Aletti 2001): best understood against **Jewish apocalyptic literature** (2 Esd./4 Ezra 5:22; 14:40; T. Levi 2.3; 2 Bar. 81.4; Qumran Hymns 1QHa 10.13; 20.13), where their purpose "is to assure the reader that the insight of the seer is from God, not that the seer himself has any special authority." Against Lincoln/Gnilka who read it as post-Pauline authority-boosting. Thielman: the claim "should not be read as weighty evidence either for or against authenticity."
- **[3:4]** τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ Χριστοῦ — *Thielman:* "the mystery about Christ" (not "the mystery that is Christ"), thinking of "the leading role that Christ plays in bringing unity to believers, according to 2:14–22."
- **[3:5]** "not made known… in other generations… as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to his holy apostles, and prophets." *Thielman* rejects the "relative/comparative" reading (Theodoret, Chrysostom, Calvin — known "vaguely" or "to few" before); with recent interpreters holds "the mystery… was wholly unknown in the past and has now been revealed," citing 3:9–10 ("hidden for ages past") and Col. 1:26.
- **[3:5]** Syntax decisions (*Thielman*): (1) ἁγίοις and αὐτοῦ modify **both** apostles and prophets, but the sandwich construction distinguishes "his holy apostles, **and** prophets" as two groups (cf. 4:11); (2) αὐτοῦ refers to **Christ** (not God), since Christ gives apostleship in 4:11 and appears at end of 3:4; (3) ἐν πνεύματι modifies the verb ἀπεκαλύφθη ("revealed **by the Spirit**"), paralleling **1 Cor. 2:6–10** (revelation "through the Spirit"), following Fee 1994.
- **[3:5]** Why apostles are called "holy" (*Thielman*): their link with the historical Jesus "sets the apostles apart… as critically important to the church's identity." Defends authenticity against Baur/Lincoln/Gnilka ("holy apostles" as subapostolic dignifying, cf. Ignatius Magn. 3.1 "holy elders"): (a) Bockmuehl 1990 — ἅγιοι in Col. 1:26 may itself denote a special group who proclaim the mystery, so Eph. 3:5 merely names them; (b) early leaders were already highly esteemed (1 Thess. 5:12–13; Gal. 2:9 "pillars"). Concedes the exact phrase "holy apostles" is "without question, unusual for Paul" (Dahl).
- **[3:5]** Who are the holy apostles and prophets? *Thielman:* "people such as Peter, Barnabas, Apollos, and certainly Paul himself, who presided over the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles" (Percy 1946).
- **[3:5, tension with 3:3/8]** Critical question: why does Paul stress his own centrality (3:2–4, 8–10) yet in 3:5 give the whole apostolic group the role? *Best (1997a):* "Probably… the author of Ephesians had not thought this problem through" — confluence of two contradictory traditions (Gospels/Acts = twelve commissioned to Gentiles; Pauline corpus = Paul uniquely commissioned). ***Thielman rejects this***, arguing 3:1–13 "reflects the complexity of the actual situation": Paul is apostle to Gentiles par excellence (Rom. 1:5, etc.; Gal. 2:7–9) yet tolerated other independent Jewish-Christian missionaries (Cephas, Apollos at Corinth); same pattern in Acts (Peter–Cornelius, Acts 10–11; 15). "Paul plays the chief strategic role… But the whole group of apostles and prophets also understood this insight (3:5)."
- **[3:6]** THE MYSTERY DEFINED — the three συν- compounds (see dedicated section below): συγκληρονόμα καὶ σύσσωμα καὶ συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας — "heirs together and one body together and sharers in the promise together" with Jewish believers, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου.
- **[3:7]** διάκονος (diakonos, "servant") of the gospel — *Thielman:* Paul serves the gospel "in the sense that he preaches it to the Gentiles." His role came "according to the gift of God's grace given to me according to the effect [ἐνέργεια] of his power [δύναμις]." Thielman distinguishes "effective power" (ἐνέργεια) from "potential power" (δύναμις), as in 1:19 and 3:20; principally Paul's **conversion** from persecutor to preacher is in view (Gal. 1:13–16). "God's great power was behind Paul's own conversion… and remains effective in his ministry despite his imprisonment."

### 3:8–13 (How Paul fulfills his task; the church and the powers)

- **[3:8a]** ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ πάντων ἁγίων (elachistoterō pantōn hagiōn, "least of all the saints") — recalls 1 Cor. 15:8–10 (Paul "least of the apostles" because he persecuted the church). *Thielman* devotes extended discussion to whether ἐλαχιστότερος (a comparative of a superlative) is a subapostolic "intensification" (Baur/Gnilka/Lincoln; the alleged trajectory 1 Cor. 15:9 "least of apostles" → Eph. 3:8 "least of saints" → 1 Tim. 1:15 "first of sinners"). **Thielman rejects this**: the term appears in the mechanical writer **Heron** (fl. Alexandria mid-60s AD, i.e. exactly when Ephesians would be written) meaning simply "least of all" in pedestrian prose; and the wickedness-escalation thesis is "even shakier" (Barn. 5.9 "is not autobiographical," doesn't mention Paul; Ignatius Trall. 13.1 ἔσχατος shows Christians independently spoke this way). Conclusion: "it seems best to excuse Eph. 3:8a from the debate over the epistle's authorship."
- **[3:8b]** Content of the gospel described as τὸ ἀνεξιχνίαστον πλοῦτος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (to anexichniaston ploutos tou Christou, "the untraceable wealth of Christ"). *Thielman:* genitive means "the grace of God shown in Christ" (not that the wealth is Christ himself). ἀνεξιχνίαστος ("untraceable") is apt because "No one would have been able to 'trace out' the logic of the Scriptures to this conclusion; God had to reveal it." Parallel to **Rom. 9–11**, where Paul calls the inclusion of "all Israel" a μυστήριον (11:25) and praises God's "untraceable" (ἀνεξιχνίαστοι) ways (11:33).
- **[3:9]** φωτίσαι πάντας (phōtisai pantas, "to illumine everyone") — πάντας is masculine, so it does NOT refer back to neuter ἔθνεσιν (Gentiles); Paul illumines "everyone, whether Jew or Gentile" about "the plan [οἰκονομία] of the mystery." Textual note (3:9): πάντας is original despite omission in א, A, etc.
- **[3:9]** Mystery described three ways: (1) ἀποκεκρυμμένος ("hidden," perfect tense emphasizing hiddenness, known only to God); (2) ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων — *Thielman* takes this as "from ages past" (temporal), NOT "from the Aeons" (personal cosmic powers), since Paul's parallel uses (1 Cor. 2:7; Col. 1:26; Rom. 16:25) describe "the massive length of time"; (3) hidden "in the God who created (κτίσαντι) all things."
- **[3:10]** ἵνα clause — purpose is **why Paul preached** (not why the mystery was hidden): "in order that the beautifully complex wisdom of God might now be made known through the church to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (see dedicated section below).
- **[3:11]** κατὰ πρόθεσιν τῶν αἰώνων — *Thielman:* "according to his purpose from before the ages" (genitive of quality / temporal), NOT "predetermination of the Aeons" (rejects Schlier's cosmic-powers reading), because τῶν αἰώνων in 3:21 is chronological and the phrase resembles 1 Cor. 2:7 (wisdom "predestined before the ages"). Predestinarian echo of 1:5, 9, 11.
- **[3:11]** ἐποίησεν ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ — *Thielman:* God "carried out" (not "made/planned") his eternal purpose in Christ. Unusual word order "the Messiah, Jesus our Lord" (ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν) with the article emphasizes "Jesus our Lord is 'the Messiah.'"
- **[3:12]** παρρησία καὶ προσαγωγὴ ἐν πεποιθήσει ("boldness and confident access") — recalls 2:18. *Thielman:* παρρησία, rooted in Athenian political free speech (Euripides), by Paul's time carried connotations of frank speech in **friendship**; here it denotes believers' free, confident speech to God, "primarily evident in prayer." διὰ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ = "faith in Christ" (Thielman, against O'Brien's "Christ's faithfulness"), because 3:17 uses the same phrase for the readers' faith.
- **[3:13]** διὸ αἰτοῦμαι μὴ ἐγκακεῖν — *Thielman:* Paul asks **his readers** (not himself; and "I ask," not "I pray") "not to be discouraged in my sufferings for you." ἐγκακέω = "be discouraged"/"grow weary" (an inner disposition, cf. 2 Cor. 4:16 and the "inner human being" of 3:16). Readers were discouraged that "the apostle to the Gentiles" had been imprisoned ~5 years (Acts 24–28), perhaps mirroring their own marginalization/refusal of the imperial cult.
- **[3:13]** ἥτις… δόξα ("inasmuch as they are your glory") — *Thielman:* rejects the common "honor/dignity" (noneschatological) reading; argues δόξα is **eschatological** — "his faithful proclamation… has led to their salvation and to a partial experience of the 'glory' that one day will be theirs in full." Variation on the theme that suffering yields glory (2 Cor. 4:16–17; Rom. 8:18), but here "the one who suffers is not the one who is glorified" (cf. 2 Tim. 2:8–10; Col. 1:24).

### 3:14–19 (Prayer for inner strength)

- **[3:14]** τούτου χάριν resumes the interrupted prayer of 3:1. Paul "bows my knees before the Father" — kneeling (not the normal standing posture) marks an "emotionally charged" prayer, adding pathos.
- **[3:14–15]** Wordplay πατέρα / πατριά ("Father" / "family"): "from whom every family (πατριά) in the heavens and on earth is named." *Thielman:* "every family in the heavens" refers to "groupings of evil spiritual powers" (rulers, authorities, powers, dominions, world rulers — 1:21; 3:10; 6:12), and naming means God "created them and demonstrated his authority over them by naming them" (cf. Ps. 147:4). God is "the powerful authority over all social groups, including the inimical spiritual powers." (Rejects Muddiman's "departed Christians" reading.)
- **[3:16]** ἵνα δῷ — main request: God "may grant you, according to the wealth of his glory (κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ), to be strengthened in power (δυνάμει) through his Spirit (διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος) in the inner human being (εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον)." *Thielman:* δόξα here connotes **power** (cf. Col. 1:11; Rom. 6:4); κραταιωθῆναι aligns with inner courage/determination (LXX).
- **[3:16]** ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος ("the inner human being") = "the interior life of the person" (cf. 2 Cor. 4:16 outer/inner contrast; Rom. 7:22–23 = νοῦς/mind). Paul prays God give readers the inner strength he himself experienced under suffering.
- **[3:17a]** κατοικῆσαι — result of strengthening: "so that Christ might dwell through faith in your hearts." *Thielman* (following Hoehner) reads the second infinitive as **result** of the first, not restatement: strengthening → Christ's indwelling. This does not imply Christ is absent; "What they apparently lack is the inner strength and encouragement they should draw from these truths" (cf. Gal. 2:19b–20).
- **[3:17b]** ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐρριζωμένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι ("rooted and founded in love") — syntactically "fraught." *Thielman:* the nominative participles function like finite indicative verbs → a "parenthetical interjection: 'You are rooted and founded in love!'" (like 2:5 "By grace you are saved!"), evidence of oral dictation. "Love" here = **God's love shown in Christ** (not believers' mutual love, nor love for God/Christ), "the fertile soil and solid foundation of the believer's life."
- **[3:18–19a]** ἵνα ἐξισχύσητε καταλαβέσθαι… καὶ γνῶναι — *Thielman:* this ἵνα clause does NOT begin a second petition but "builds on the immediately preceding clause and gives the reason why Paul wants Christ to dwell in his readers' hearts." ἐξισχύω connotes "growing in power to the point of prevailing"; the picture is "a struggle to prevail over ignorance or confusion."
- **[3:18]** The four dimensions τὸ πλάτος καὶ μῆκος καὶ ὕψος καὶ βάθος ("breadth and length and height and depth") — object left grammatically missing ("the line goes dead… interpretive pandemonium"). *Thielman* surveys views (Origen: four points of the cross; Ambrosiaster: perfect sphere; Bengel/Eadie: dimensions of the temple/church; Schlier: heavenly inheritance; Gnilka/Arnold: polemical). He adopts **view 3** (Chrysostom, Westcott, Aletti, MacDonald): "primarily a reference to the vastness of divine love (v.19a)" while "in the background… lies Paul's concern with God's administrative plan, his mystery, and his complex wisdom (vv. 9–10)." Supported by σὺν πᾶσιν τοῖς ἁγίοις ("with all the saints"), recalling the σύν- language of 2:19–21 — Christ's love "is best comprehended 'with all the saints,' in all their social variety."
- **[3:19a]** γνῶναι τὴν… ἀγάπην τοῦ Χριστοῦ τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν τῆς γνώσεως ("to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge") — rhetorical wordplay know/knowledge; readers "could not understand the massive magnitude of Christ's love apart from God's revelation."
- **[3:19b]** ἵνα πληρωθῆτε εἰς πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ θεοῦ ("that you might be filled up to all the fullness of God") — climactic purpose, not a third petition. εἰς = "up to"/extent (temporal nuance), paralleling 4:13 (reaching "a mature man… the fullness of Christ"). *Thielman:* readers "are in the process of becoming all that God created them to be… Just as God is perfect, so one day they too will be perfect."

### 3:20–21 (Doxology)

- **[3:20]** τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ("Now to the One who is able") — *Thielman:* not a merely formal traditional feature; it "draws these threads together" — God's power (δύναμις) is a prominent theme (1:19; 1:20–2:10; 3:7; 3:16). God is able ὑπὲρ πάντα… ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ ("beyond everything, infinitely more than what we ask or imagine"). ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ appears first in all Greek here and in 1 Thess. 3:10; 5:13.
- **[3:20]** κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν τὴν ἐνεργουμένην ἐν ἡμῖν ("according to the power at work in us") — wordplay δυναμένῳ/δύναμιν; parallels 1:19; Paul is "probably thinking of God's power at work… in terms of the Spirit" (Fee).
- **[3:21]** αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ("to him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus") — *Thielman:* the church makes God's glory known because "its very existence as a multiethnic community… testifies to God's beautifully complex wisdom (3:10)." "No thought here of the church as equal to Christ or prior to Christ"; emphasis on "the unity of Christ and the church." (Textual note 3:21: scribes dropped καί or reversed order to avoid implying church = Christ; the harder reading "in the church and in Christ Jesus" is original.)
- **[3:21]** εἰς πάσας τὰς γενεὰς τοῦ αἰῶνος τῶν αἰώνων ("for all the generations of the age of the ages") — verbose combination of two stock formulas; coherent as "a single age… of a series of ages and… all generations." ἀμήν = Paul's own "final, heartfelt expression that what he has said is true" (not necessarily a cue for congregational response).

## Mystērion (3:1–13) — Thielman's background argument in full

**Definition and content.** *Thielman:* the mystery here (3:6) is narrower than at 1:9–10. In 1:9–10 the mystery is "the summation of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, in Christ"; here it is "one part of that grand scheme—the unification of two formerly separated ethnic groups in one body through the gospel." The narrowing reflects the digression's purpose: Paul describes his own administrative responsibility (οἰκονομία, 3:3) within God's administration (οἰκονομία, 1:10). Crucially the mystery is not merely Jewish–Gentile *unity* but their **equality**: "not merely the unity of Jews and Gentiles in the worship of the one God but their equality with each other (2:11–12)."

**Background — apocalyptic revelation, not mystery cult.** *Thielman* consistently frames μυστήριον through the lens of **Jewish apocalyptic revelation** rather than Greco-Roman mystery cults:
- The mechanism of its disclosure is **revelation** (κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν, 3:3), explicitly compared to **Daniel 2:17–19** — Daniel receiving the content and interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's dream "apart from any cleverness of his own, and strictly because God in his mercy revealed it to him." "No amount of exegetical study of the Scriptures would have yielded this insight."
- First-person insight claims (3:4) are located in "Jewish apocalyptic literature" and the Qumran Hymns (following Aletti), where their function is to assure the reader "that the insight of the seer is from God."
- The mystery was "hidden" (ἀποκεκρυμμένος, perfect tense) ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων. Thielman explicitly weighs and **rejects** the reading "from the Aeons" (i.e. personal cosmic/spiritual powers) in favor of the temporal "from ages past," citing Paul's parallel usage in 1 Cor. 2:7; Col. 1:26; Rom. 16:25 where αἰών denotes "the massive length of time." (He notes αἰών "was beginning to take on connotations of a personal cosmic power in the first century" but judges "Any other connotation here is unlikely.") — *This is the closest the slice comes to weighing the mystery-cult / cosmic-powers background against the apocalyptic-temporal one; Thielman decides for the apocalyptic-temporal (Jewish rāz-type) sense.* [NB: the transliterated term "rāz" itself does not appear verbatim in this slice; Thielman's background category is expressed as "Jewish apocalyptic literature," Daniel, Qumran, 1 Cor. 2.]

**Genuinely new element.** *Thielman* addresses the objection that Gentile inclusion was already anticipated in the OT (Isa. 45:14; 60:1–16; Hag. 2:7; Ps. 68; cf. 1QM 12.13–15; Tob. 13:11; Pss. Sol. 17.30). His answer: OT/Second-Temple texts expected Gentiles to be *included in the worship of God* and even to *serve Israel* in the eschatological restoration, but "The full equality of Gentiles with Jews in a newly constituted humanity… was not revealed previously." "The previously unknown element lies in the σύν." He adds (following **Grindheim 2003**) that the achievement of unity "by means of setting aside the Mosaic law (2:14–15)… was certainly unanticipated in any known form of pre-Christian Jewish expectation."

**Wisdom connection.** The mystery, once revealed through the church, displays "the beautifully complex wisdom of God" (πολυποίκιλος σοφία, 3:10) — linking μυστήριον to the wisdom-of-God-in-creation theme (Prov. 8; Job 28; Sir. 42–43; 1QHa).

---

## Church and the powers (3:10) — full detail

**Text:** "in order that the beautifully complex wisdom of God might now be made known **through the church** to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (τοῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις)."

- **Purpose-clause logic:** *Thielman* takes the ἵνα as giving the reason why **Paul preaches** (v.8–9), not why the mystery was hidden. "He does this to make something known" — namely God's wisdom, to the powers.
- **πολυποίκιλος σοφία (polypoikilos sophia):** a rare term combining ποικίλος ("many-coloured, dappled, manifold") + πολύς. Connoted "complex variety" — a multicolored veil (Euripides), a floral wreath of many flowers, complex emotions/reasoning. Thielman glosses "beautifully complex" / "very many-sided" (BDAG), and suggests a hint of God's unfathomable wisdom in creation (Prov. 8:22–31; Job 28; Sir. 42–43; Bar. 3; Wis. 8; 1QHa). The wisdom is "especially evident in the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in the church (v.6)" — "the 'creation' of a 'new human being' (2:15–16)."
- **αἱ ἀρχαὶ καὶ αἱ ἐξουσίαι (hai archai kai hai exousiai, "the rulers and authorities"):** *Thielman* identifies these as **thoroughly evil spiritual beings** who "exercised power over the unbelieving world" (2:1–2; 6:12). He invokes the Second-Temple **Watchers tradition** on Gen. 6:1–6 — heavenly beings who "strayed from the place in heaven that God had assigned to them at creation" and introduced humanity to wickedness including magical arts (CD-A 2.17–21; 4QEnoch; 1 En. 6–16; T. Naph. 3.4–5; behind 1 Pet. 3:19–20; Jude 6; 2 Pet. 2:4–5) as possible background.
- **The cosmology (core claim):** "By its very existence as a unified body… the church makes known to the evil spiritual rulers and authorities the vastness of God's creative wisdom: he not only created the universe with its endless variety, but in a wholly surprising way he has also begun to restore the crowning achievement of his creation—humanity—to its original unity."
- **Spatial/victory framework:** the powers occupy the same "heavenly" (ἐπουράνιος) realm as God, Christ, and believers (1:3, 20; 2:6), but are "conquered and beneath the Messiah's feet" (1:20–22). Since the church is one with the enthroned Christ (2:6), "the powers are also… beneath the church's feet." "From this position with Christ, the church can 'now' (νῦν) testify to the powers that… their designs will ultimately fail." The church's witness is proclamatory testimony from a position of victory, not persuasion.
- **First-century application (Thielman):** for Christians in Roman Asia, "the earthly rulers and authorities—the deified and reigning emperors… worshiped in the imperial cult"—would have seemed "evidence of the continuing potency of the evil heavenly powers." Paul's claim that "the church provides counterevidence of God's superior power would come as a welcome encouragement."
- **Predestinarian anchor (3:11):** the making-known to the powers was "according to his purpose from before the ages, which he carried out in the Messiah, Jesus our Lord."

## Named scholars / positions cited (representative)

- **Best (1997a, 1998):** proposes 3:5 = confluence of two contradictory traditions; "the author… had not thought this problem through." *Thielman disputes.* Also on nominative participles (3:17b) functioning as finite verbs; on textual variants.
- **Lincoln (1982, 1990):** reads Paul's insight-claim (3:4), "holy apostles" (3:5), and ἐλαχιστότερος (3:8) as post-Pauline/pseudonymous markers. *Thielman disputes each.*
- **Gnilka (1971):** pseudonymity, authority-boosting, wickedness-escalation. *Disputed.*
- **Baur (2003 [19th c.]):** 3:5 as increasing reverence over time. *Disputed.*
- **Aletti (2001):** apocalyptic background of first-person insight-claims; view 3 on the four dimensions (Christ's love + wisdom/plan). *Followed.*
- **Bockmuehl (1990):** ἅγιοι in Col. 1:26 may denote a special mystery-proclaiming group. *Used to defend authenticity.*
- **Grindheim (2003):** unity achieved by setting aside Mosaic law was unanticipated in pre-Christian Judaism. *Followed.*
- **Hoehner (2002):** structure of 3:16–19 (second infinitive = result); ἐξισχύω; four dimensions = Christ's love. *Largely followed.*
- **O'Brien (1999):** διὰ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ = "Christ's faithfulness" (3:12). *Weighed, rejected in favor of "faith in Christ."*
- **Fee (1994):** ἐν πνεύματι modifies the verb (3:5); Spirit as power (3:16, 20). *Followed.*
- **Percy (1946):** identity of the holy apostles/prophets. **Schnackenburg (1991), Schlier (1957), MacDonald (2000), Muddiman (2001), Arnold (1989), Deichgräber (1967), Aune (1997)** all cited on syntax, doxology form, and the four-dimensions debate.
- **Patristic:** Origen (four points of the cross; "incorrect" grammar of 3:17b; unfamiliarity with συμμέτοχα), Chrysostom (view 3 seed; δόξα as honor), Theodoret & Theophylact (relative reading of 3:5; ambiguity of 3:13), Calvin (four dimensions = Christ's love), Ambrosiaster (perfect sphere), Irenaeus/Gregory of Nyssa/Augustine (cross).

---

## Notable Greek terms with glosses (as given by Thielman)

- **μυστήριον** (mystērion) — the hidden divine plan of Jewish–Gentile equality in one body, revealed by God (3:3, 4, 9); "mystery about Christ."
- **οἰκονομία** (oikonomia) — 3:2/3:8 = Paul's God-given **responsibility** of administering; 3:9 = God's **administrative plan**; root sense "management of a household," linked to -οἰκ- words of 2:19–22.
- **ἀποκάλυψις / ἀπεκαλύφθη** (apocalypsis) — revelation / "was revealed"; the **means** by which the mystery came (κατά = by means of).
- **συγκληρονόμα, σύσσωμα, συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας** (synklēronoma, syssōma, symmetocha tēs epangelias) — "heirs together, one body together, sharers together in the promise" (3:6); the three συν- compounds echoing 2:19–22. σύσσωμα "appears here for the first time in all known literature… possibly Paul invented it." συμμέτοχα = intensified μέτοχος. ἐπαγγελία = the Abrahamic promise merging with the promised eschatological Spirit (Gal. 3:14).
- **ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι** (archai kai exousiai) — "rulers and authorities"; evil spiritual beings in the heavenly places (3:10).
- **πολυποίκιλος σοφία** (polypoikilos sophia) — "beautifully complex / very many-sided wisdom" of God (3:10).
- **ἀνεξιχνίαστος** (anexichniastos) — "untraceable" (wealth of Christ, 3:8; cf. Rom. 11:33).
- **ἐπουράνιος** (epouranios) — "heavenly (places)" (3:10), occupied by God, Christ, believers, and the powers alike.
- **διάκονος** (diakonos) — "servant" of the gospel (3:7).
- **ἐνέργεια / δύναμις** (energeia / dynamis) — "effective power" vs "potential power" (3:7, 20).
- **παρρησία καὶ προσαγωγὴ ἐν πεποιθήσει** (parrēsia kai prosagōgē en pepoithēsei) — "boldness and confident access" (3:12), rooted in friendship/free-speech, evident in prayer.
- **ἐγκακέω** (enkakeō) — "be discouraged / grow weary" (3:13).
- **ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος** (ho esō anthrōpos) — "the inner human being," the interior life (3:16; = νοῦς, Rom. 7).
- **κραταιωθῆναι** (krataiōthēnai) — "to be strengthened" (inner courage/determination, 3:16).
- **πατήρ / πατριά** (patēr / patria) — "Father / family," the naming wordplay (3:14–15).
- **ἐρριζωμένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι** (errizōmenoi kai tethemeliōmenoi) — "rooted and founded" (in love, 3:17b), nominative participles functioning as an interjection.
- **πλάτος, μῆκος, ὕψος, βάθος** (platos, mēkos, hypsos, bathos) — "breadth, length, height, depth" (3:18); object left unstated.
- **πλήρωμα** (plērōma) — "fullness" of God (3:19b); becoming all God created them to be (cf. 4:13).
- **ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ** (hyperekperissou) — "infinitely more than" (3:20); a near-neologism (also 1 Thess. 3:10; 5:13).
- **δοξα / doxology form** — four-part Hellenistic-Jewish/Christian pattern (recipient, glory, duration, amen) per Aune/Deichgräber.

## Overflow (lines 554–603 — belongs to next slice, §VIII 4:1–16)

Brief flag only: the slice runs past 3:21 into the intro of **§VIII "The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)."** Content covered there: 4:1–16 as the hinge linking chs. 1–3 and 4–6; the "one new human being" (2:15) and temple "under construction" (2:21–22); vv.1–6 practical admonitions + seven affirmations of unity; vv.7–16 gifts given by **Christ** (δόματα, not χαρίσματα) via a modified Ps. 67:19 LXX; the five offices of 4:11 (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers). Opens the **post-Pauline-authorship debate on church structure**: MacDonald/Schnackenburg/Zimmermann read the "routinization of charism" and narrowing to teaching offices as post-Paul; *Thielman rebuts* by showing the messy, non-linear development of early church order (Gal. 6:6 "instructor"; Didache 15; Ignatius; Justin 1 Apol. 65, 67; Origen on Eph. 4:11), concluding structure cannot date a text. **This material should be assigned to and extracted by the slice covering 4:1–16; not developed here.**
